content:
Post-training climbed maths, code and tool use on process data written by humans or
synthesised under their direction, and that ladder is running out of rungs. The next rung
is research, and research closes the loop: a system that can do research can work on its
own training. That makes research plausibly the last capability we have to teach directly,
and discovery the bottleneck on intelligence itself, not a place to apply intelligence
once it is finished.
Table of Contents
01 Post-training lived off borrowed process data. Research is where that ends.
02 Agents look like they can do research. The benchmarks say otherwise.
03 AI already accelerates the rest of science.
04 Self-improvement closes on a verifier. World models stand in where it is expensive.
05 Four problems next: environments, verifiers, world models, failures.
01 Scale the scientific environments, not just the scientific data
02 Verifiers robust enough to be optimised against
03 Domain world models where feedback is genuinely expensive
04 Learning efficiently from the loop's own failures
01 The ceiling
Post-training has been living off process data someone else already produced.
Post-training gains so far form a ladder. First maths. Then code. Then tool use, the
agentic turn. Every rung worked for the same two reasons: a large body of human process
data already existed for it, or could be synthesised cheaply under human direction; and
the result could be checked automatically.
Fig. 1. Each rung had a corpus someone else had already generated
and something could check automatically. The research rung does not. The artefact worth
learning from is the whole design → verify → revise loop, including everything that
failed, and it is almost never written down.
My claim is that this ladder is running out of rungs of that kind. Human text, and
synthetic text generated under human direction, is not where the next order of magnitude
comes from. To keep getting smarter, models will increasingly have to train themselves.
A system that trains itself is doing research.
Research ability stops being one capability among many and becomes the constraint on all
the others. It also differs from them in kind. A system that can run the research loop
can point it at its own training, which makes research plausibly the last
capability we have to teach directly.
That has not happened yet, as the next section shows. But every capability so far has had
to be handed over. Research is the one that would end the handing over.
02 The gap
Agents look like they can already do research. Every benchmark that isolates it says otherwise.
Frontier agents write training code, launch runs, read checkpoints and report numbers. It
has the shape of automated research. Measured directly, it isn't yet.
Measured directly Three benchmarks that isolate research ability.
Benchmark Score What was measured
PostTrainBench
23.2%
best agent post-training a base model end to end, against 51.1% for the official instruct model [1]
AI4AI-Bench
0.250
best system rewriting a training algorithm , with hyperparameter tuning factored out (mean 0.166) [3]
ASI-Bench
26.6
project-level research score once the method is no longer given, down from 50.9 with full guidance [6]
The last is the most diagnostic. ASI-Bench [6]
progressively withdraws human methodological guidance inside the same project :
the method is supplied, then only named, then left for the agent to choose. The score
falls by almost half as the guidance is withdrawn, step by step. The missing half was
the human's.
What today's models have is engineering strength, not research strength. An analysis of
a large corpus of released post-training
trajectories [2] separates the two.
Execution-level capability is iterating inside a chosen strategy;
strategy-level capability is revising that choice as evidence arrives.
Agents are strong at the first. At the second, the strategy is locked in at the start of
the run and the entire remaining budget goes to local adjustment inside it.
That pattern is also what agents have been scoring on. Earlier suites could be won by
collecting more data or tuning hyperparameters, and none of them separated a change in
how a run is executed from a change in how the model learns . AI4AI-Bench
takes tuning off the table: the agent has to rewrite the training algorithm itself, and
the rewrite is rerun from scratch under an evaluator the agent never sees. The best
system closes only a small fraction of the distance between the existing algorithm and
the optimum. [3]
The same analysis tries the three obvious fixes, and all three fail. Experience-driven
scaffolding lifts execution sharply and leaves the strategy exactly where it was. Human
guidance redirects the strategy, and the agent falls back into local adjustment as soon
as training starts. More inference compute helps on easy tasks and buys almost nothing
on the hardest. What is missing is not experience, guidance or reasoning compute. It is
a mechanism for spontaneously re-evaluating the strategy mid-run .
An environment would have to teach exactly that, and it is not "write better code". It
is: notice, halfway through, that the plan is wrong, and change it. It cannot be learned
from write-ups, because a write-up is the format from which the abandoned plans have
been removed.
The environment has to be a real one: live scientific repositories, executable pipelines,
genuine failure. The loop closes on itself. Models need science to keep improving, and
the improving is itself done by doing science.
03 The other direction
AI is already accelerating the rest of science.
The argument so far is internal to AI. The second motivation points outward, and 2026
made it concrete.
In mathematics, OpenAI reported a proof that solutions to the Navier–Stokes equations can
blow up in finite time: roughly ten thousand agents over 88 hours, plus a further 17
hours for a model to formalise the
result. [7] [8]
In biology,
Anthropic reported that Claude produced optimised implementations of 36 open-source
biomolecular models in under four weeks, including a new set of triangle-attention
kernels, for about a 4× average speed-up. [9] The
supervisors were two people with no prior kernel-engineering background.
Every lab running those models now waits a quarter as long: a compounding gain across an
entire field, from a capability AI already has. Science is full of bottlenecks shaped
like that.
04 The design
Recursive self-improvement is the right shape. The verifier closes it. A world model makes the verifier affordable.
Human judgement is the scarcest input in the research loop. Every step that requires it
caps the throughput of the whole system; that is the real content of the ASI-Bench result
above. The design target is a loop that runs with as little human intervention as
possible.
Recursive self-improvement is the right shape for a boring reason: an RSI loop needs two
components, not an agent that is already good at the domain. A proposer
generates the next hypothesis. A verifier decides whether the last one
worked. "Accumulate experience, including failures" is an empty instruction unless
something can tell the loop that an attempt failed, and ideally why. Failures carry as
much information as successes, often more — but only once something has called them
failures. The verifier is not an implementation detail of the loop. It is what makes the
loop a loop, and its verdicts are the only signal the proposer is ever trained on. A
system built this way should get better at the task the longer it runs. The proposer is
allowed to start out poor. The verifier is not.
The loop has an obvious problem: its throughput is set by its most expensive edge, and
that edge is verification. Outside maths and code the verifier is rarely a unit test. It
is reality itself: a training run, a simulation, an assay. An agent can propose ten
thousand protein designs in an afternoon. Verifying ten thousand designs at the bench is
not an afternoon, may not be a year, and may not be affordable at all. The proposal side
scales and the verification side does not, and the surplus proposals are wasted.
Fig. 2. Everything the proposer learns arrives as the verifier's
verdict, and the question is where that verdict goes. An ordinary experimental loop
returns a revised candidate. An RSI loop returns a revised proposer , which is
exactly the strategy-level revision that today's agents were found not to
do [2] . The verifier is also the loop's expensive
edge, and the world model sits on that edge alone: it stands in for the verifier on most
candidates, turning an unaffordable verification problem into an affordable one, and the
ground truth that does get measured flows back to sharpen the stand-in. In ML research the
analogue is predicting a run's outcome without paying for
the run [10] [11] ;
in biology the canonical instance is the virtual
cell [12] .
A world model earns its place on exactly that edge. It is not a second
mechanism alongside the verifier. It is a cheap approximation of the verifier: a fast
in-silico predictor of what the real verification would return, used to triage which
candidates are worth spending the real verifier on. It does not have to be right. It has
to be cheap and better than chance.
Biology shows what this looks like taken seriously, because there the verifier is a
wet-lab assay. Arc Institute's virtual-cell programme predicts what a cell does under a
perturbation it has never seen, so millions of perturbations can be screened before
anything is pipetted. [12] Their 2026 challenge
raises the bar to zero-shot prediction across unseen cell
lines. [13] It is the right bar: a stand-in that
only works on contexts the real verifier has already measured buys no new science. The
same structure recurs inside AI research, where the verifier is a training run: a
persistent model of the research process predicts what the run would show, so compute
goes to the experiments worth
running. [10] [11]
The two pieces of the design are not peers. The verifier closes the loop, and because its
verdict is the only signal the proposer learns from, it is the objective the proposer is
optimised against. The world model is conditional. It matters where the verifier is too
expensive to run on every candidate; there it stands in on most of them, and each turn of
the loop becomes cheap enough for the loop to improve often.
05 What matters next
Four problems, in the order I would attack them.
01 Challenge Scale the scientific environments, not just the scientific data
If research ability is the constraint, the direct lever is agentic data and environments
drawn from real science. ScienceIDE [14] names the
obstacle a scientific experience bottleneck : repositories encode decades of
method, but fragmented toolchains, implicit domain conventions and specialised
correctness criteria keep that knowledge from becoming learnable experience. Their answer
is to convert repositories into executable environments with expert-defined acceptance
criteria, then train on verified trajectories.
They also report transfer: scientific experience improved not only held-out
scientific-code repair but general code, reasoning and knowledge benchmarks. If that
holds at scale, science is not a vertical application of foundation models. It is a
training signal for them. The domain benchmarks show how much headroom is left: 17% on
real bioinformatics analyses in BixBench [15] , and
the guidance-withdrawal collapse in ASI-Bench [6] .
02 Challenge Verifiers robust enough to be optimised against
Once an agent can search against a verifier, the verifier is the objective.
Yukon [16] shows the upside: open autoresearch
challenges in quantum circuit optimisation, proof-system acceleration and GPU kernels,
where every submission must clear a deterministic gate before it is merged, and the
frontier ratchets. Its ECDSA.fail challenge reports beating the Google Quantum AI
benchmark by 62%.
The downside arrives the moment the gate is weaker than the optimiser.
KernelBench-Verified [17] documents frontier models
exploiting the narrow test distribution, in one case with a "ReLU kernel" that checks
whether the input shape matches the test configuration and returns the input unchanged.
Gimlet Labs put a number on it: KernelBench overstates correctness by
31%. [18] On a benchmark that is embarrassing. In a
live RSI loop it is worse than embarrassing, because the false result becomes training
signal.
Fuzzing does not close this, for the reason the same write-up gives: testing can only
examine a finite subset of an effectively infinite space, and the agent is optimising
against whatever harness you chose. Formal verification has to move into the verifier
itself. The pieces exist. Symbolic equivalence checking of generated kernels via SMT
proved 16 of 26 Triton kernels and caught two that passed numeric tests while being
mathematically inequivalent [18] . In
repository-scale joint implementation-and-proof synthesis, the best agent still only
closes 27 of 43 instances [19] . There are
machine-checked proofs of the properties production systems actually rely on, such as
permutation equivariance and correctness of
tiling [20] . None of them is ready to sit inside a
loop running millions of proposals. That gap is the problem.
03 Challenge Domain world models where feedback is genuinely expensive
In fields where a single round of feedback costs weeks and real money, wet-lab biology
among them, the world model is not an optimisation. It is the precondition for running
the loop at all. The argument in §04 takes concrete form here: a research world model
for the research process itself [10] , virtual
cells for perturbation biology [12] [13] ,
and predictive architectures general enough to be retargeted across
domains [21] . The open question is calibration,
not accuracy: a filter is useful when you know where it is trustworthy, and dangerous
when you don't.
04 Challenge Learning efficiently from the loop's own failures
In an unfamiliar environment an agent's first attempts are bad, and most of what the loop
produces is failure. An RSI system earns its name only if that exhaust becomes
capability. The design question is what, exactly, gets updated.
CAKE [22] is the clearest worked example I know in
a domain I care about. It treats the compiler as part of the agent harness under
evolution, not a fixed black box. Recurring failures are promoted into verifier rules,
IR primitives, model calibrations and reusable tactics: "shrink the search space using
what went wrong", precisely. A parallel line of work makes the same move on the
model–harness pair. One alternates weight and harness
optimisation [23] . Another evolves the harness,
retaining matched successes, regressions and near misses as verified sibling
trajectories for the next model update [24] . A
third composes typed operators over data, harness and weights under one loop
kernel [25] .
What I take from these is that the unit of self-improvement is not the model. It is the
whole system: model, harness, verifier, search space. The open problem is how to
co-evolve them without the loop quietly optimising one of its own measuring instruments.
